---
title: Fréchet-differentiability and C¹-smoothness
---

Two notions of smoothness for $f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ on an open interval $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, and the surprising way [[concepts/o-minimal-structures|o-minimality]] collapses the gap between them. (HW2 Ex 0.11.)

## Fréchet-differentiable

$f$ is **Fréchet-differentiable at** $x \in I$ if there is a linear map $Df(x) : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ (in one variable, just a number $f'(x)$) such that

$$
\lim_{h \to 0} \frac{\lvert f(x+h) - f(x) - f'(x)\,h \rvert}{\lvert h \rvert} = 0 .
$$

In one dimension this is exactly ordinary differentiability: $f'(x) = \lim_{h\to 0} \frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}$ exists. $f$ is Fréchet-differentiable **on** $I$ if this holds at every $x \in I$, yielding a derivative function $f' : I \to \mathbb{R}$. (In $\mathbb{R}^n$ the distinction from the weaker *Gâteaux* / directional derivative matters; on an interval it does not.)

## C¹-smooth

$f$ is **$C^1$-smooth** on $I$ if it is Fréchet-differentiable on $I$ **and** its derivative $f' : I \to \mathbb{R}$ is **continuous**.

So $C^1$ asks for two things — differentiability *plus* continuity of the derivative. The second is a genuinely extra requirement: differentiability everywhere does **not** imply $f'$ is continuous.

## The gap: differentiable ≠ C¹

The standard counterexample is

$$
f(x) = \begin{cases} x^2 \sin(1/x), & x \ne 0 \\ 0, & x = 0. \end{cases}
$$

  <text x="292" y="168" class="lbl6 ital" text-anchor="end">0</text>
  <text x="470" y="92" class="lbl6" fill="#f59e0b">±x²</text>
  <text x="486" y="210" class="lbl6 ital" fill="#3b82f6">f(x)=x² sin(1/x)</text>
  <g transform="translate(60,292)">
    <text x="0" y="0" class="leg6">differentiable at 0 (f′(0)=0, trapped by ±x²), but f′ oscillates in [−1,1] near 0 → not C¹</text>
  </g>
</svg>

It is differentiable everywhere: away from $0$ by the chain rule, and at $0$ because $\lvert f(h)/h\rvert \le \lvert h\rvert \to 0$ gives $f'(0)=0$. But for $x \ne 0$,

$$
f'(x) = 2x\sin(1/x) - \cos(1/x),
$$

and $\cos(1/x)$ oscillates through $[-1,1]$ as $x \to 0$, so $\lim_{x\to 0} f'(x)$ does not exist and $f'$ is discontinuous at $0$. Thus $f$ is Fréchet-differentiable but **not** $C^1$.

## The o-minimal regularity phenomenon

The counterexample above is **not definable** in any [[concepts/o-minimal-structures|o-minimal structure]] — its derivative $\cos(1/x)$ has infinitely many oscillations near $0$, violating the finiteness ([[concepts/monotonicity-theorem|monotonicity]]) that o-minimality forces. This is no accident:

> **Phenomenon (HW2 Ex 0.11).** If $f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ is **definable** in an o-minimal structure and Fréchet-differentiable on $I$, then $f$ is automatically $C^1$-smooth.

The reason: a definable $f'$ is, by the [[concepts/monotonicity-theorem|monotonicity theorem]], piecewise continuous and monotone with only finitely many breakpoints, and at each candidate breakpoint the one-sided limits of $f'$ exist (no infinite oscillation is possible). Differentiability pins those one-sided limits to the actual derivative value, so $f'$ can have no jumps — it is continuous. More is true: definable functions are piecewise $C^r$ for every $r$, so "differentiable" already drags the regularity all the way up.

**Without definability the phenomenon fails** — $x^2\sin(1/x)$ is precisely the witness. So the implication "everywhere-differentiable $\Rightarrow C^1$" is a feature of [[concepts/tame-geometry|tame geometry]], not of analysis in general.
